cells.tense: You are holding more than one true thing at once, and it is working right now.
cells.ask: Tomorrow, take one thing you see clearly and say it plainly to the person it concerns, then let their reply change it.
cells.core:
You can hold several true things at once without dropping any. You notice how much of what crosses the table is real — an edge in a voice, a detail that doesn't line up, what isn't being said. None of it reads as noise to you.

What keeps that from turning into fog is the adjusting underneath. You shift while you go — more of this, less of that, read it again in a minute — and it's the moving that keeps things steady rather than any fixed position. What this balance can feed next is plain speech: one thing you see, said out loud while you're still unsure of it, and what comes back allowed to help decide whether it holds.

cells.place: reading a stream that keeps moving while you stand in it

cells.tense: There is a room ahead where you have already found the words for all of it.
cells.ask: Before one conversation, write down the single point you'd be willing to lose, and go in carrying only that.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is a version where you've found the words for it all — the whole clear picture, people caught up, nothing left unsaid. You're living in that room already, so the conversation in front of you reads as a rehearsal you keep failing.

Nothing is wrong with your instrument. You see more, not less; the abundance is real. The trouble is that you haven't picked first — which position you'll stand behind, which direction, which one line you'll actually say. The reading runs in a loop while one eye stays on a room that hasn't formed yet. One true thing chosen out loud is worth more here than the whole free map in your head.
cells.sheetLine: You already have the words. Pick what they're for.

cells.tense: You used to tell one kind of true from another, and that edge is behind you now.
cells.ask: When one question sits with you unmarked, take it to one person and say what the answer would cost if it came.
cells.core:
At its best this is a read that lands and the mind moves on — one thing noticed, tested against the next moment, kept or dropped without ceremony. That was ordinary for you, and some of it still is.

What you have now is more true things than you can place. The known and the guessed sit on the same shelf, and nothing quite settles — not because the instrument is gone, but because the sharp edge that separates one kind of true from another has gone quiet.

So put one item in front of someone you trust and ask them to place it. That kind of work tends to happen in a mind that isn't already full of yours.
cells.sheetLine: You know more than you can place. Bring it to someone.

cells.tense: You are reading the moment as it comes, and you call that just being practical.
cells.ask: Next time you notice a detail and smooth it over, say it out loud — briefly, as something you noticed, not advice.
cells.core:
The reading is happening — the timing, the space you leave for someone's feelings, the moment to stay quiet, what will land and what won't. It runs continuously, and people feel things steady because of it.

But you'd say you were just handling things. The work is already in your hands; what hasn't been claimed is what is guiding them.

Here's what it costs. A good read that stays invisible can't be checked. Nobody can tell you you're wrong about the room, so your version of it goes unchallenged. Say one thing you notice, out loud, and let it be looked at. That isn't the same as taking credit — and it doesn't break what works.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading the room. Say one thing you see.

attempts.check: The draft wants to say what the person is really doing underneath — steering, choosing, calibrating — but the record only says how abundantly they are knowing, not what they do with it. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not aware of a stream of knowing at all; I just help people' and the cell would have nothing left. The asks survive that: telling one true thing plainly, choosing one and naming it, handing a question to someone, taking back credit, all hold even if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything that makes a reader of them — that flatters the seeing instead of handing over the settling.
